
Fecal samples from control hares had an average of `r fecal[food == "Control", round(mean(CP_dm, na.rm = TRUE), 2)]` ± `r fecal[food == "Control", round(sd(CP_dm), 2)]`% protein, `r round(fecal[food == "Suppl.", mean(CP_dm, na.rm = TRUE)] - fecal[food == "Control", median(CP_dm)], 2)`% less than samples from food supplemented hares (p = `r pfood`, t = `r tfood`, df = `r dffood`, R2 = `r round(rsq(foodmod), 2)`; Figure 1F). Fecal samples collected in January were `r round(fecal[m == 1, median(CP_dm)] - fecal[m == 3, median(CP_dm)], 2)`% higher in protein than those collected in March (p = `r pfec`, t = `r tfec`, df = `r dffec`, R2 = `r round(rsq(fecmod), 2)`). Using the `r fecfor[, .N]` cases where fecal samples were collected from a hare with weekly foraging data, fecal protein showed a slightly negative response to foraging effort (p = `r pfecfor`, t = `r tfecfor`, df = `r dffecfor`, R2 = `r fecforR2`).

The linear mixed model that tested how snowshoe hare fecal protein content was influenced by environmental conditions and food supplementation found that available twig biomass (t = `r t_biomass`) and the interaction between temperature and food (t = `r t_tempint`) significantly influenced foraging (Table 2). Neither hare density (t = `r t_density`) nor mortality rate (t = `r t_mort`), nor their interactions with food treatment, affected foraging rate according to the model (Table 2). The model found that as twig availability increased from `r biopred[, min(x)]` to `r biopred[, max(x)]` kg/ha, fecal protein increased from `r biopred[x == min(x), round(mean(predicted), 1)]`% to `r biopred[x == max(x), round(mean(predicted), 1)]`% (β = `r b_biomass` ± `r se_biomass`, CI[-0.03, 0.08]  Figure 3A). While fecal samples from food supplemented had `r b_food` ± `r se_food`% higher protein than controls across the range of twig availability, there was no difference between the two groups' responses to twig biomass (t = `r t_food`, Table 2). There was a significant interaction between food treatment and ambient temperature. As weekly temperatures increased from `r min(temppred$x)` to `r max(temppred$x)`°C, food supplemented hares increased their fecal protein by `r round(temppred[food == "Suppl." & x == max(x), predicted] - temppred[food == "Suppl." & x == min(x), predicted], 2)`%, always staying above the 10% threshold, while control hare fecal protein decreased  by `r abs(round(temppred[food == "Control" & x == max(x), predicted] - temppred[food == "Control" & x == min(x), predicted], 2))`%, from `r round(temppred[food == "Control" & x == min(x), predicted], 2)`% to `r round(temppred[food == "Control" & x == max(x), predicted], 2)`% (Figure 3B). This model explained roughly 20% of the variance within fecal protein content (Marginal R2 = `r Q1R2m`).
